runs.analysis: Candidate A has the full 9 assumptions and 9 failure modes. They cover governance, architecture, budget, geotechnical/seismic, political, cost escalation, workforce, environmental, and energy risks. Each has plan-specific numbers, tripwires, playbooks, and stop rules, and the risk scores are computed correctly. Its flaws are that FM3 (ridership) is mislinked to A3 (budget), A3 and A6 overlap, A1 contains a timeline inconsistency (September 2026 mobilization), and it is verbose. Candidate B has only 6 assumptions and failure modes, with non-contiguous IDs (A1, A2, A3, A7, A8, A9), so it looks like follow-up content was dropped. It is cleanly mapped one-to-one, factually accurate on gauges, and adds distinct risks (supply chain, flooding and insurability). It omits seismic/geotechnical, environmental, energy, and workforce risks, and its tripwire and warning-sign lists are thinner. A's broader coverage and richer detail outweigh its mislink, so A wins narrowly.

The two candidates differ mainly in completeness and coverage.

Completeness and format: A has only six assumptions and six failure modes, and its IDs jump from A3 to A7. A4–A6 appear to have been dropped, perhaps by the duplicate-ID guard, which leaves a visible gap. B has all nine assumptions and nine failure modes with consistent IDs.

Coverage: A covers prototype validation, political commitment, budget, supply chain, rail gauge and interoperability, and flooding and insurability. It omits geotechnical and seismic risk, workforce, environment, and energy, which are major risks for a deep-sea Gibraltar tunnel. B covers governance timeline, structural validation, ridership, geotechnical and seismic, political commitment, cost escalation, workforce knowledge loss, cetacean and environmental oversight, and energy. It omits flooding and insurance, and it overlaps in places (A2/A4 and A3/A6).

Specificity and correctness: A's assumptions and triggers are numerically crisp. However, its early warning signs often restate the failure triggers while its tripwires are stricter, which inverts the usual order. A also wrongly says Spain's AVE network is Iberian gauge when it is already 1,435 mm, and FM5 rests on that error. B is plan-specific and dated, with milestones such as boreholes in March 2027 and the prototype in March 2028. Its tripwires are properly staged and its risk scores are arithmetically consistent. B has minor inconsistencies: A1 pairs an 18-month ratification timeline with September 2026 mobilization, and the FM3 revenue figures do not match the earlier €500M–1B projection.

Downstream usefulness: B's broader, scheduled set of risks and tripwires gives later stages more to work with. A is sharper per item but leaves out several core risk areas.

Overall, B is more complete and more diverse, with only minor flaws. A is crisp but incomplete and has a factual error.

Candidate A delivers nine distinct assumptions (A1–A9) and nine distinct failure modes. Each one is tied to its own root-cause assumption and has detailed stories, tripwires, playbooks and stop rules. The content is specific to the plan, covering RTE lead times, land holding costs, workforce, PUE, DGSI, latency, permitting, tenants and financing. It has flaws. Some numbers are questionable. The holding cost of €50–75k/ha over 18 months across 12,880 ha gives roughly €1B, not €6–9B. The playbook for FM4 suggests concealing PUE shortfalls from tenants. Some details are invented, such as Eemshaven. It is still complete, internally structured, and useful for downstream stages.

Candidate B is badly flawed. The assumptions table repeats A1–A3 three times and A4–A6 twice, so the same entries are duplicated. This is exactly the kind of re-emission the guard was meant to drop. The failure modes repeat as well. "The Buffer Budget Black Hole" appears three times (FM1, FM4, FM7), with FM4 and FM7 mislabeled with root cause A1 even though the story concerns A2. "Local Mandate Backlash" appears twice. The risk entries are inconsistent. A5, A6 and A8 have no failure modes, and FM2 is scored 25/25. The tripwires and playbooks are thinner, with fewer quantified thresholds. Because of the heavy duplication, B has only about five unique failure modes, and it is much less useful.

A is clearly better.

Candidate A is badly degraded by duplication. The assumptions table repeats A1–A3 three times and A4–A6 twice, which suggests the guard against repeated IDs did not work. Only 9 distinct assumptions exist, but the table has many more rows. Failure modes FM1, FM4 and FM7 are identical copies titled "The Buffer Budget Black Hole". FM4 and FM7 are labelled root cause A1 but their content concerns A2. FM3 and FM5 are also duplicates. So A has only about 6 distinct failure modes, and several are mislabelled. Some content is weak or internally inconsistent: the stop rule for FM3 uses PUE 1.25, which contradicts the 1.20 target. FM1 gives an unbudgeted cost of "€1.3B" with no derivation. FM6's "currently commissioned 100 MW" is an invented detail. A does have some good points, such as the A9 yield-differential assumption and the 2 ms RTT latency issue.

Candidate B has 9 distinct assumptions and 9 distinct failure modes (A1–A9 map one-to-one). They cover grid, land holding cost, workforce, cooling/PUE, DGSI, latency, permitting, tenants and financing. The content is concrete, with numbers, tripwires and pivot options such as downsizing to 3 GW, a single cluster, or leaving the region. That matches the prompt's red-team spirit.

B has flaws. The holding cost arithmetic is dubious: €50–75k/ha × 12,880 ha × 1.5 years = €0.97–1.45B, not €6.44–9.66B. That error runs through FM2. FM4 also includes an unethical playbook line, "do not disclose PUE shortfalls to tenants". Some stories are very long. Even so, B is far more useful and complete than A, and its distinct coverage outweighs its errors.

Candidate A delivers nine distinct assumptions (A1–A9) and nine distinct failure modes, each with a detailed story, early warning signs, tripwires, a three-step playbook and a stop rule. The coverage is broad: budget reallocation, latency, cost opacity, accessibility, liability pivot, float exhaustion, distributor adoption, governance gridlock and resource cannibalization. It is plan-specific and decision-useful. It has some flaws. Some timeline and number inconsistencies appear, such as the Month 6 and Month 14 confusion in FM4 and the mention of the "2026 elections". Some risk scores are also arguable. The 5% royalty cap is described inconsistently as a cap on costs. None of this undermines the document's overall usefulness.

Candidate B is badly degraded. Its assumptions table repeats A1–A3 three times, and A4–A6 twice. Its nine failure modes are just three unique ones repeated three times each, so FM1, FM4 and FM7 are identical. Its A5 trigger also contains a corrupted character ("„100 Million"). It does have some good ideas, such as dated validation methods and a Three Strikes enforcement assumption, but the duplication makes it largely useless and it fails the stage's format. It also appears to ignore the guard against repeated ids. Its A7–A9 assumptions have no corresponding failure modes.

A is clearly better.

Candidate A is badly degraded. Its Assumptions table repeats A1-A3 three times, so A4-A9 are mixed in with duplicates. One row also has a corrupted "„100 Million" and then repeats with a fixed "€100 Million". The failure modes are only three distinct scenarios (Liability Deadlock, Latency Choke, Royalty Rebellion) copied three times, as FM1/4/7, FM2/5/8 and FM3/6/9. The follow-up assumptions A4-A9 (Three Strikes enforcement, budget, OSDM capacity, public awareness, governance, clearing float) have no failure modes of their own. That means the stage's guard against repeated IDs failed. The result has little coverage, many redundant sections and no value for downstream stages. FM9 also changes the archetype label for the same scenario.

Candidate B has nine distinct assumptions and nine distinct failure modes. They cover budget reallocation, latency, cost opacity, accessibility/PRM, the liability pivot, float exhaustion, distributor adoption, governance gridlock and resource cannibalization. Each is tied to the plan's details (SNCF/DB/ÖBB, Trainline/Omio, €300M reserve, 90-minute threshold, the corridors) and has specific tripwires, playbooks and stop rules. Its weaknesses are some length, a few minor inconsistencies (e.g., the "Month 6 → Month 14" timeline confusion, a hydrogen reallocation story that is speculative, and "2026 elections" as a trigger) and a likelihood/impact calculation that is slightly off in places (16 labelled CRITICAL, which is correct as ≥15). Overall B is far better.

Candidate A is much more specific and decision-useful. Its assumptions are concrete and testable (contingency reserve, health-authority MOU, contractor bid ceiling, cooling-center infrastructure, canvassing success rate, alert-threshold calibration, triage reliability, employer adoption, paper-registry GDPR risk). Each has a dated validation method and a quantified failure trigger. The failure stories use plan-specific numbers and details (€300k reserve, 1,000 units, 60% contact rate, Leipzig-Grünau, Saxony, Month 4 gate), and the tripwires, playbooks and stop rules are mostly measurable and sensible. Risk scores are computed correctly. Weaknesses: several validation deadlines fall before the plan date of 2026-05-03 (04-15, 04-30, 05-01), there are minor internal oddities (92% described as "marginally meeting" a 95% target, muddled budget arithmetic in FM1), it has no assumption on transport surge, comms reach or NGO liability, and joint owners blur accountability. Candidate B covers a more diverse set of risks (alert-declaration authority, transport surge, NGO liability, CRM audit, analog-media enrollment, internal department capacity) and has clean single owners and correct risk math. But its content is thinner and more generic, with vague triggers. Some playbooks are illogical or counterproductive: FM1 suspends all cooling centers to preserve capital after a governance delay, and FM2 diverts 80% of the home-intervention budget to transport. FM9's story is confusingly worded, some figures are invented without grounding (2,000 units, 200% surge), and the stop rules are less actionable. On balance, A's depth, quantification and grounding outweigh its date and consistency flaws, and B's broader coverage does not make up for its weaker response logic.

Candidate A has nine assumptions spread across governance authority, installation contractors, health MOU, internal staff reallocation, CRM audit, analog enrollment, transport surge, NGO liability, and procurement price escalation.
- Strengths: Transport surge, NGO liability and volunteer safety, and supplier pricing are real risks from the plan, and B leaves these out. The A1 assumption (director's authority within normal municipal powers) ties to the no-new-legislation constraint. Dates are future-facing and risk scores are consistent.
- Weaknesses: The failure stories are thinner and more generic. FM9's story is muddled (it says the assumption "proves true" when it means it is false). FM4 is a weaker, peripheral risk. Some playbooks are odd, such as FM2 re-allocating 80% of the home-intervention budget to transport, and FM1 suspending all cooling-center contracts. It does not cover worker protection or alert-threshold calibration, both explicit scope items. It shows less city-specific grounding.

Candidate B has more quantified assumptions, each with a concrete validation test.
- Strengths: Validation methods name sample sizes, thresholds, and cost limits (€150 per unit, 200 residents, 15 clinicians). Failure stories give plausible mechanisms with figures and sequences, and cover cooling-center infrastructure limits, alert-threshold calibration, daytime canvassing bias, the contingency reserve (MCR), worker protection, and GDPR paper-registry risk. Playbooks are decision-useful, with explicit cost thresholds and fallback paths. It is grounded in Leipzig and Saxony. Risk arithmetic is correct.
- Weaknesses: Several validation deadlines and tripwire dates fall before the stated current date of 2026-05-03 (04-15, 04-30, 05-01). FM7 says a 92% audit result "meets the 95% target marginally", which is an error. It uses "ADA", a US term, for a German city. Joint ownership is less clear than a single owner. It omits transport surge and NGO or volunteer safety. It is very verbose.

Overall, B is more insightful, specific, and useful to downstream stages, and it covers more of the plan's scope areas. Its past-dated deadlines and a few logic slips cost it points. A is cleaner on dates and covers transport and NGO risks, but its stories are more generic and one is confused.
